pos: n. (the Wurttemberg Cistercian abbey of 1147, the most complete medieval monastic complex north of the Alps, a Protestant seminary from 1556)
etymology: German Maulbronn, the mule's spring, from the founding legend of a mule that found water.
biblical_def: Maulbronn in Wurttemberg was founded in 1147 and is the most completely preserved medieval monastic complex north of the Alps: church, cloister, refectories, lay brothers' hall, infirmary, mill, forge and the elaborate water system that served them all, substantially intact. In 1556, after Wurttemberg turned Lutheran, Duke Christoph converted it into a Protestant seminary, one of the lower schools feeding the Tubingen Stift, and in that capacity it educated Johannes Kepler, Friedrich Holderlin and Hermann Hesse, who set Unterm Rad in its corridors. The dictionary records Maulbronn as the best thing that happened to a dissolved abbey anywhere in Europe. The buildings were not plundered or converted into a nobleman's house; they were turned into a school where boys were taught Greek and Hebrew and the Scriptures, which is the one use that answers the purpose the founders half-intended. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) is the charter of such a place, “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) its timetable, and “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) the reason for the languages.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education; a cloister as a covered walk in a monastery; a refectory as a room for meals; a preceptor as a teacher; and erudition as learning.
webster_full: SEMINARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a covered passage or walk round a court, usually with a colonnade.
REFECTORY, n. A room of refreshment; a hall or apartment in convents, where they take their meals.
PRECEPTOR, n. A teacher; an instructor; the principal of a school.
ERUDITION, n. Learning; knowledge gained by study, or from books and instruction.

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Wurttemberg Cistercian abbey of 1147, preserved almost entire, converted in 1556 into a Protestant seminary that taught Kepler and Holderlin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a monastery's best second use is a school. Maulbronn's cloister became a place where boys construed Greek, and the apostolic command behind that is “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15), whose verb concerns dividing a text rightly.

The live temptation is to treat the conversion as cultural vandalism dressed as piety. It was the opposite: the fabric survived because it was still being used for something, and what it was used for was “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13). The languages were taught because of the claim made for the writings, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), so that congregations could do what the Bereans did, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11).

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey near Tubingen, founded 1183, a Protestant school from 1560)
etymology: Old High German, Bebo's houses; the abbey lies in the Schonbuch forest.
biblical_def: Bebenhausen in the Schonbuch forest north of Tubingen was founded in 1183 by Rudolf of Tubingen, first for Premonstratensians and almost immediately for Cistercians, and it became one of the wealthiest houses in Swabia. Its summer refectory and the filigree spire of its chapter are of the first quality. Wurttemberg suppressed it at the Reformation, and from 1560 it served as one of the duchy's Protestant monastery schools, teaching boys destined for the ministry; later it was a royal hunting lodge, and after 1946 the provisional parliament of Wurttemberg-Hohenzollern met in its refectory. The dictionary records Bebenhausen beside Maulbronn, because together they show that the Wurttemberg settlement was deliberate policy rather than accident. The duchy took the great abbeys and made them into a ladder of schools feeding a university divinity faculty, which is a serious answer to the question of what a Protestant church does with the plant it inherits. “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) and “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) are the commands it answers, and “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17) explains why ministers were the product.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chapter house is given under chapter as an assembly of monks; a lodge as a small house in a park; a refectory as a room for meals; a ministry as the office of a minister; and divinity as the science of divine things.
webster_full: CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the monks of a convent, or of a religious order; the place of such assembly.
LODGE, n. A small house in a park or forest; a temporary habitation; a hut.
REFECTORY, n. A room of refreshment; a hall or apartment in convents, where they take their meals.
MINISTRY, n. The office, duties or functions of a subordinate agent of any kind; ecclesiastical function.
DIVINITY, n. The science of divine things; the science which unfolds the character of God and the doctrines of revelation.

corruption_summary: Wealthy Swabian Cistercian abbey of 1183, suppressed at the Reformation and used from 1560 as a Protestant school for intending ministers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a reforming church must answer the question of training. Wurttemberg turned its abbeys into schools and its schools into a supply of preachers, and Paul's charge is exactly that order: “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) before exhortation and doctrine.

The live temptation is to think a recovered gospel needs no institutions. It needs men who can read, which is why “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) is commanded in the same breath as faithfulness. The mechanism makes the preacher indispensable, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and the charge laid on him is “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

pos: n. (the Black Forest abbey founded 1095 under the Hirsau reform, whose schoolboys' papers survived under the floor)
etymology: German Alpirsbach, from a stream name of uncertain origin in the upper Kinzig valley.
biblical_def: Alpirsbach in the Black Forest was founded in 1095 by three Swabian nobles and settled from St Blasien under the Hirsau constitutions, and it keeps an austere Romanesque church with almost no ornament — the Hirsau reform expressed in stone. It passed to Wurttemberg and became a Protestant monastery school. In the 1950s restorers lifting the floorboards of the dormitory found a hoard of paper and cloth that had fallen through the gaps over centuries: Latin exercises, letters home, a love note, scraps of clothing, drawings, the discarded litter of generations of schoolboys, now the richest surviving archive of its kind in Germany. The dictionary records Alpirsbach for that hoard, because it is the ordinary human texture that histories of the Reformation usually omit. Boys who were being trained to preach also drew pictures and complained about the food. The gospel is addressed to such people and not to an ideal: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28) names its hearers, and “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) their standing, since “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) applies to a diligent boy and an idle one alike.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dormitory as a sleeping room; an exercise as a task for improvement; litter as scattered rubbish; austere as severe and rigid; and a scholar as a learner.
webster_full: DORMITORY, n. A place, building or room to sleep in; a gallery in convents divided into several cells.
EXERCISE, n. Use; practice; the exertions and movements customary in the performance of business; a task for improvement.
LITTER, n. Scattered rubbish; straw or other soft substance used as a bed for horses.
AUSTERE, a. Severe; harsh; rigid; stern; applied to persons or their manners.
SCHOLAR, n. One who learns of a teacher; one who is under the tuition of a preceptor; a pupil; a disciple.

corruption_summary: Black Forest abbey of 1095 built to the austere Hirsau pattern, later a Protestant school, whose pupils' papers survived beneath the dormitory floor.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel addresses actual people. The Alpirsbach floor gave up love notes and bad Latin, and the invitation Christ issues is pitched at exactly that population, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28) — the labouring and the laden, not the exemplary.

The live temptation is to tell the history of reform as a story of heroes and systems. The hoard under the boards corrects it. Every boy in that dormitory stood on the same footing, “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), because “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) levels the diligent and the idle. What was asked of them afterwards was James' plain religion, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27).

pos: n. (the Rheingau Cistercian abbey of 1136, the largest wine estate in the Holy Roman Empire)
etymology: German Eberbach, the boar's brook; the abbey lies above Eltville in the Rheingau.
biblical_def: Eberbach in the Rheingau was settled in 1136 by monks sent from Clairvaux at Bernard's direction, and it became the greatest wine producer in the Holy Roman Empire, working vineyards along the Rhine, running its own fleet of river barges, and keeping a press house whose medieval beam presses still stand. Its monks' dormitory and the long vaulted lay brothers' refectory are among the finest Cistercian interiors in Germany. The abbey was secularised in 1803 and the vineyard continues as a state domain. The dictionary records Eberbach for the wine, because the Cistercian economy is where the medieval system is least open to caricature. These were men who cleared ground, trained vines, built presses and kept accounts, and the work was good work. Scripture honours it directly and never calls it second-rate: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) is said over any honest trade, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17) is the prayer for it, and “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) is the word for a bad season.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vineyard as a plantation of vines; a press as an instrument for squeezing; a vintage as the produce of the vine for a season; a cellar as a room under a house; and husbandry as the business of a farmer.
webster_full: VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes; an inclosure or yard for grape vines.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed, crushed or forced into a more compact form.
VINTAGE, n. The produce of the vine for the season; the grapes or fruit gathered.
CELLAR, n. A room under a house or other building, used as a repository of liquors and provisions.
HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground.

corruption_summary: Rheingau Cistercian abbey settled from Clairvaux in 1136, the largest wine estate in the Empire, secularised in 1803.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the goodness of ordinary productive work. Eberbach's monks trained vines and built presses, and Paul's promise is laid on labour as such, “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58), with the Psalmist's prayer over it, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).

The live temptation is to suppose that work inside a cloister is of a higher order than work outside one. Scripture knows no such ranking. The exhortation for a failed vintage is given to every Christian, “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9), and the wisdom of working in company is proverbial and not monastic, “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.” (Ecc 4:9).

pos: n. (the Eifel Cistercian abbey founded by Bernard in 1134, dissolved 1802, refounded 1922, closed 2017)
etymology: German Himmerod, from Hemmenrode, the clearing of Hemmo; rod is a woodland assart.
biblical_def: Himmerod in the Eifel was founded in 1134 by Bernard of Clairvaux himself, who is said to have chosen the site personally, and it became a substantial house with granges across the Moselle country. It was dissolved in the secularisation of 1802 and the church was demolished for building stone. In 1922 Cistercians returned, and between 1952 and 1960 they rebuilt the abbey church to the surviving eighteenth-century plans. In 2017 the community, reduced to a handful of elderly monks, was dissolved again, and the buildings passed to the diocese of Trier. The dictionary records Himmerod for that three-part history, because the modern closure is the plainest possible commentary on the institution. A house founded by the greatest Cistercian of all, destroyed, rebuilt with great effort in the twentieth century, and closed for want of men within sixty years. Scripture does not promise permanence to any arrangement of ours: “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) is the standing expectation, “a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10) the thing actually promised, and “Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.” (Heb 13:8) the only continuity there is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines secularisation is given under secularise as conversion to common use; dissolution as the act of breaking up an assembly; to refound is given under found as to lay the basis; a community as a society of persons; and permanence as continuance in the same state.
webster_full: SECULARIZE, v.t. To make secular; to convert from spiritual appropriation to secular or common use.
DISSOLUTION, n. The act of dissolving; the separation of a body into its parts; the breaking up of an assembly.
FOUND, v.t. To lay the basis of any thing; to set, or place, as on something solid for support.
COMMUNITY, n. Common or joint possession; a society of people having common rights and privileges.
PERMANENCE, n. Continuance in the same state, or without any change that destroys the form or nature of a thing.

corruption_summary: Eifel Cistercian abbey founded by Bernard in 1134, dissolved 1802, refounded 1922, rebuilt in the 1950s and closed again in 2017.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no institution of ours is promised a future. Himmerod was founded by Bernard, levelled, rebuilt at great cost, and closed for lack of men, and Hebrews states the expectation without cruelty: “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

The live temptation is to read the 2017 closure as a verdict on faith in general rather than on a particular arrangement. The promise was never attached to the arrangement. It is attached to a city “a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10), held by people whose description is “strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13), and resting on the only unchanging thing there is, “Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.” (Heb 13:8).

pos: n. (the Rhineland abbey founded 1189 where Caesarius wrote the Dialogue on Miracles)
etymology: German Heisterbach, the beech-sapling brook, from Heister, a young beech.
biblical_def: Heisterbach in the Siebengebirge above the Rhine was founded in 1189 as a daughter of Himmerod, and its great church was demolished after the secularisation of 1803, leaving the famous ruined apse that became a favourite subject of Rhine Romanticism. Its lasting product is a book. Caesarius of Heisterbach, prior and novice-master, wrote about 1220 the Dialogus Miraculorum, a dialogue between a monk and a novice containing some seven hundred and fifty stories — visions, demons, deathbeds, hosts that bled, souls in purgatory, a famous tale of a monk who listened to a bird for what he thought was an hour and found three hundred years had passed. It is the richest single source for what ordinary medieval Christians actually believed. The dictionary records Heisterbach for the Dialogus, with gratitude as a historical source and no credulity at all. The stories were told to form novices, and that is the problem. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) is the duty they bypass, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) the authority they displace, and “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17) the means they substitute for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an exemplum is given under example as a pattern; a vision as something imaginary seen in a dream; a novice as one newly admitted to a religious order; credulity as a readiness to believe without evidence; and a legend as a chronicle of saints' lives.

NOVICE, n. One who is new in any business; one newly admitted to membership in a religious house.
CREDULITY, n. Easiness of belief; a disposition or readiness to believe without sufficient evidence.
LEGEND, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints, formerly read at matins.

corruption_summary: Rhineland Cistercian abbey of 1189 where Caesarius wrote the Dialogus Miraculorum about 1220, the richest source for popular medieval belief.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that edifying stories are not a basis for doctrine. Caesarius collected seven hundred and fifty of them to train novices, and the duty his method bypasses is the one Paul gives everyone, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). The authority it quietly displaces is “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16).

The live temptation is to treat the Dialogus as charming medieval colour. It was catechesis, and it taught purgatory and bleeding hosts to young men as fact. Paul's warning fits the whole genre, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8) — a tradition of men — and the means God appointed instead is plain, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17).

pos: n. (the Westerwald Cistercian abbey of 1212, with one of the earliest German Gothic churches)
etymology: German Marienstatt, the place of Mary; the house was named for its dedication.
biblical_def: Marienstatt in the Westerwald was founded in 1212 by monets sent from Heisterbach and settled on its present site in the Nister valley in 1222. Its church, begun in 1227, is among the earliest buildings in Germany to adopt the French Gothic system wholesale, and it was completed and has been in continuous use for most of the period since; the abbey was dissolved in 1803 but recovered by Cistercians in 1888 and remains a working monastery with a school attached. The dictionary records Marienstatt for its dedication, because the name states the thing the Reformation could not leave alone. A house called the place of Mary, with a Marian liturgy at its centre, has put a creature where Scripture puts Christ. The dictionary says this of a community it has no wish to insult, and says it plainly because the matter is not negotiable: “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11) admits no second foundation, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28) is addressed by Christ to the burdened in His own name, and “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) leaves no office of intercession to be filled.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dedication as the act of consecrating to a divine Being; mediation as interposition between parties; intercession as prayer on behalf of another; invocation as the act of calling upon in prayer; and a creature as a created being.
webster_full: DEDICATION, n. The act of consecrating to a divine Being, or to a sacred use, often with religious solemnities.
MEDIATION, n. Interposition; intervention; agency between parties at variance, with a view to reconcile them.
INTERCESSION, n. Prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
INVOCATION, n. The act or the form of calling for the assistance or presence of any being, particularly of some divine being.
CREATURE, n. That which is created; every being besides the Creator, or every thing not self-existent.
scriptures: For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
corruption_summary: Westerwald Cistercian abbey of 1212 with one of the earliest fully Gothic German churches, dissolved 1803 and recovered in 1888.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the singularity of the foundation. Paul leaves no room for a second: “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11). A liturgy ordered around a creature's intercession has supplied what that sentence excludes, however pious the intention.

The live temptation, in an age that prizes agreement, is to treat this as a difference of emphasis. It is not. Christ issues the invitation Himself and in His own name, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28), and the verdict He secures admits no supplement, “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). What a sinner needs is given entire in “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8).

pos: n. (the Harz Cistercian abbey of 1127 whose monks engineered the mining waters, a Protestant school from 1570)
etymology: German Walkenried, from a personal name with ried, a reedy place or a clearing.
biblical_def: Walkenried on the southern edge of the Harz was founded in 1127 and became one of the wealthiest Cistercian houses in Germany, with more than four hundred monks and lay brothers at its height. Its distinctive work was hydraulic: the monks drained the Goldene Aue, and in the Harz they built ponds, ditches and channels to drive and dewater the silver mines, laying the foundation of the system later developed as the Oberharz water regale and now recognised as a monument of pre-industrial engineering. The abbey accepted the Reformation; its last abbot turned Lutheran, and from 1570 the buildings housed a Protestant school. The cloister and chapter house survive largely intact. The dictionary records Walkenried for the water channels and the school together. Men who dug drainage ditches for silver mines and men who taught Latin in the same cloister were doing work of the same dignity, which is the Reformed estimate exactly: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) covers both, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17) is prayed over both, and “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9) is said of both without distinction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hydraulics as the science of fluids in motion; a sluice as a frame of boards for stopping water; drainage as the act of draining; a mine as a pit from which metals are taken; and a calling as a vocation.
webster_full: HYDRAULICS, n. That science, or branch of science, which treats of the motion of fluids, and the art of conducting water.
SLUICE, n. The stream which flows through a flood gate; a frame of boards to stop and let out water.
DRAIN, v.t. To filter; to cause to pass through some porous substance; to empty by drawing off gradually.
MINE, n. A pit or excavation in the earth, from which metals and minerals are taken.
CALLING, n. A divine summons or invitation; vocation; profession; trade; the usual occupation.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
corruption_summary: Wealthy Harz Cistercian abbey of 1127 whose monks engineered the mining water system, which accepted the Reformation and became a Protestant school in 1570.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that there is no hierarchy of callings. Walkenried's brothers cut drainage channels for silver mines and later its rooms taught Latin, and Paul's promise covers both equally, “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58), with one prayer over both, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).

The live temptation is the old division between a sacred vocation and a secular trade, which the lay-brother system institutionalised and the Reformation dismantled. Peter settles it in four words addressed to everybody, “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9). The wisdom of working together is ordinary and needs no habit, “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.” (Ecc 4:9).

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey near Hanover, Lutheran since 1593 and still an Evangelical abbey with a preachers' seminary)
etymology: From the Low German place name Lucca or Loccum, probably a marsh or wood name.
biblical_def: Loccum, west of Hanover, was founded in 1163 by Count Wilbrand of Hallermund and settled from Volkenroda. What distinguishes it from every other house in this group is that it never stopped. The community accepted the Reformation gradually and formally became Lutheran in 1593, retaining its abbot, its chapter and its buildings, and it has continued as an Evangelical abbey ever since; since 1820 it has housed the preachers' seminary of the Hanoverian church, where candidates for the Lutheran ministry complete their training, and the abbot of Loccum remains an office in that church. The Romanesque and early Gothic church, cloister and chapter house are intact. The dictionary records Loccum as the one full answer in this run to the question of what becomes of a monastery under a recovered gospel. It became a place where preachers are made. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) is the charge the seminary exists to serve, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17) the reason such a place is needed, and “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7) the pattern of one generation teaching the next.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education; a candidate as one who seeks an office; ordination as the act of conferring holy orders; a chapter as a corporation of clergymen; and continuance as a remaining in the same state.
webster_full: SEMINARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university.
CANDIDATE, n. One who seeks or aspires to some office or privilege; one who offers himself for a place.
ORDINATION, n. The act of conferring holy orders or sacerdotal power; called consecration.
CHAPTER, n. A corporation or community of ecclesiastics belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church.
CONTINUANCE, n. A holding on or remaining in a particular state; permanence in the same state.
scriptures: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
corruption_summary: Cistercian abbey near Hanover, founded 1163, Lutheran since 1593 and still an Evangelical abbey housing the Hanoverian preachers' seminary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Reformation's answer to the monastery was a seminary. Loccum kept its walls and changed its business to making preachers, and the charge such a place exists to serve is “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

The live temptation is to think a recovered gospel is self-propagating and needs no training. Paul says otherwise, naming the mechanism, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and the preparation, “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13). Hebrews gives the shape of the handing on, “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7), where what is followed is a faith and not an office.

pos: n. (the Brunswick Cistercian abbey of 1145, Protestant from the Reformation, its church still in use)
etymology: German, the houses of Riddag, from the knight whose land endowed it; now a district of Brunswick.
biblical_def: Riddagshausen, now a quarter of Brunswick, was founded in 1145 by the knight Riddag and settled from Amelungsborn. Its church, built between about 1216 and 1275, is an unusually pure example of the austere Cistercian plan in brick and stone, with a straight-ended choir and a ring of chapels, and it is notable for acoustics that have made it a concert church. The abbey accepted the Reformation under the dukes of Brunswick, served as a Protestant school and then as a preachers' seminary, and the church remains in use by the Lutheran congregation. Its monks had drained and farmed the surrounding land and built the ponds that still lie around it. The dictionary records Riddagshausen as the last entry in this group, and lets it stand for the whole. A Cistercian church built for a choir of monks became a parish church where a congregation hears preaching, and that transition is the Reformation in one building. “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) names who is now in the room, “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40) authorises how they are arranged, and “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16) states what is meant to happen to them there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a choir as the part of a church for the singers; a congregation as an assembly met for worship; acoustics as the doctrine of sounds; a parish as the precinct of a church; and edification as instruction and improvement.
webster_full: CHOIR, n. A band or collection of singers; the part of a church appropriated to the singers.
CONGREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
ACOUSTICS, n. The doctrine or science of sounds, teaching their cause, nature and phenomena.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the inhabitants who belong to the same church.
EDIFICATION, n. Improvement and progress of the mind, in knowledge, in morals, or in faith and holiness.
scriptures: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
corruption_summary: Brunswick Cistercian abbey of 1145, austere in plan, Protestant since the Reformation and still in use as a Lutheran church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is who the room is for. A Cistercian choir was built for monks saying offices; the same building now holds a congregation hearing preaching, and Scripture's requirement is about that gathering, “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25).

The live temptation is to think the change merely administrative, a new tenant in an old shell. It is a change of purpose. The arrangement is licensed by “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40), the aim is stated as “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16), and the reason the room must be arranged for hearing at all is “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17).
